paras: The lynching of Epifance (also printed as Epifanio) was the hanging of a Mexican man described as a "noted" horse thief by about thirty masked men near Smithville, Arizona Territory, on or about June 26, 1882. He was taken from a deputy sheriff and a district attorney who were escorting him from Fort Thomas, and the lynchers were reported to be "supposed to be Mormons." A short wire version of the story ran in papers from New York to Seattle, often under headlines naming Mormons as the lynchers.

According to a dispatch from Fort Thomas dated June 27, the prisoner had just returned from Tucson, where he had been in the hospital under treatment for a gunshot wound in the head. The papers called him a "noted Mexican horse thief" but did not name a specific theft or charge against him.

Deputy Sheriff G. A. Stevens and the district attorney, named as Bolon in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and as P. J. Bolan in the Arizona papers, set out from Fort Thomas with the prisoner in the morning. About two miles from Smithville, the party was stopped by about thirty masked men, who took the prisoner and hanged him on the spot. The dispatch does not say where the hanging took place beyond its distance from Smithville, what time of day it was, or whether the officers resisted.

The fuller dispatch reported that "the citizens generally commend the act" and hoped it would serve as a warning to others. No report of an inquest, an arrest or any official inquiry appears in the coverage, and the identification of the lynchers as Mormons was never more than a supposition.

Two versions of the story circulated. A fuller dispatch, naming the officers, the size of the band, the prisoner's wound and local approval, appeared in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union on June 28 and later in three Arizona papers: the Phoenix Herald, the Arizona Weekly Citizen of Tucson, which ran it as a special, and the Pinal Drill. A shorter San Francisco wire item, which said only that "officers" had left Fort Thomas and that "a band of masked men" hanged the prisoner, ran on June 28 in the Salt Lake Herald, the Savannah Morning News, the New-York Tribune and the Eureka Daily Sentinel, among others.

Headline writers outside Arizona emphasized the supposed Mormon lynchers: the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer titled the item "Lynched by Mormons," the New-York Tribune "A Horse Thief Hanged by Mormons," and the Bismarck Tribune "Hung by Mormons." The Bismarck Tribune also listed the story in its wire summary as "A Greaser Horse Thief Lynched," using a slur for Mexicans. The Phoenix Herald and the Pinal Drill dropped the Mormon line altogether, while the Arizona Weekly Enterprise reduced the story to a single sentence among its editorial brevities. None of the versions questioned the lynching, and the item was still being reprinted in Louisiana's St. Landry Democrat in late July.

The date rests on the June 27 dispatch's "yesterday" and on the Silver State's "Monday," which point to June 26, but the Arizona Weekly Enterprise said the prisoner was taken "Tuesday." Nearly every version placed the lynching two miles from Smithville, but the Bismarck Tribune printed "Twenty-five miles." The St. Paul Daily Globe placed Smithville in "Utah," while the datelines of all other versions are Fort Thomas or Thomas, Arizona Territory.

bases: About thirty masked men took a prisoner from a deputy sheriff and district attorney and hanged him as a horse thief (A1, A18).

A band of about thirty masked men with no lawful authority took the prisoner from officers and hanged him; the papers frame it as punishment of a 'noted' horse thief, which 'citizens generally commend' (A1, A16, A18).

Every version, including the Arizona papers, traces to one Fort Thomas dispatch of June 27 in a fuller and a shorter form (A1, A6, A18); the Arizona Weekly Enterprise brief (A17) adds no independent detail beyond a differing day.

framing.detail: The fuller dispatch reported that citizens 'generally commend the act' and hoped it would be a warning, without dissent.
Eastern and Midwestern papers ran the short wire under headlines such as 'Lynched by Mormons' and 'A Horse Thief Hanged by Mormons'.
The Bismarck Tribune's wire summary headline called the victim 'A Greaser Horse Thief'.

conflicts.note: Spelling variants of one prisoner; the Arizona papers give Epifanio.
The dated dispatch is the nearer source; the Enterprise weekly may have used the dispatch date.
Only one paper has twenty-five; likely a misprint.
All datelines are Fort Thomas, Arizona.
